hints: Picture the Y-shaped antibody in your mind. Where exactly do antigens bind, at the two tips of the arms or on the stem?
Cutting at the hinge region separates the two arms from the stem. Which of those pieces still carries a complete variable region for binding?
walkthrough:
**Recall the antibody shape**

Think of a normal antibody as a Y shape. It is made of 2 heavy chains and 2 light chains.

The two tips of the Y are the variable regions. These are the antigen-binding sites, one on each arm.

**See what the hinge cut does**

The hinge is the flexible middle where the arms join the stem. Hydrolysis here is the classic papain digestion.

It cuts the Y into 3 separate pieces: 2 identical arm pieces called Fab fragments, plus 1 stem piece called the Fc fragment.

**Count the binding pieces**

Each Fab fragment contains one complete antigen-binding site from one arm tip, so it can still bind antigen.

The Fc stem has no variable region, so it cannot bind antigen. That gives 2 binding fragments out of 3.

options.A: Not correct. The two arm fragments keep their variable regions, so binding is not completely lost.
options.B: Not correct. There is one binding site on each arm, so cutting off both arms gives two binding fragments, not one.
options.C: Correct. The two Fab arm fragments each bind one antigen, while the single Fc stem fragment cannot bind.
options.D: Not correct. All three pieces are not the same. Only the two Fab pieces bind, the Fc stem does not.
